summary.text: Daughter of Iobates of Lycia and wife of Proetus — Homer names her Anteia (Antia), Apollodorus and Hyginus Stheneboea — who lusted for Bellerophon at Tiryns, failed to seduce him, and sent him to her father bearing a sealed death-token; not to be confused with the Arcadian Stheneboea whom Apollodorus elsewhere makes a daughter of Apheidas or Aleus.

story.text: When Proetus was driven from Argos he fled to Lycia and married the daughter of King Iobates; Apollodorus names her Stheneboea. After he returned and fortified Tiryns, the purified exile Bellerophon came to his court — and the queen lusted madly for the upright guest, yet could in no wise prevail upon wise-hearted Bellerophon, for that his heart was upright.

So she made a tale of lies, telling Proetus to slay Bellerophon or die himself. Wrath seized the king, yet awe of murdering a suppliant stayed his hand: he graved baneful tokens in a folded tablet and sent the hero to Lycia, bidding him show them to his own wife's father, that he might be slain. Homer calls the queen Anteia; Apollodorus and Hyginus call her Stheneboea — one woman, two names in the tradition.

Hyginus adds that when she heard Bellerophon had married her sister Philonoe and won half the Lycian kingdom, Stheneboea killed herself out of love and shame at her rebuff — the queen's false charge answered by the hero's triumph and her own ruin.

Apollodorus also records an Arcadian Stheneboea — daughter of Apheidas, or in another passage sister of Aleus — given in marriage to Proetus. That genealogical rival must never share this star: the wife of the lying letter is Iobates' daughter from Lycia, not a princess of Tegea.
